## Reinforcement-learning models of the Iowa Gambling Task

::: status
preprint in preparation · [code and full write-up on GitHub](https://github.com/AlejandroHinojosa2005/IGT-Modeling)
:::

The **Iowa Gambling Task** asks people to draw cards from four decks. Two decks pay well at first but lose money over time, and two pay less but come out ahead. The task is widely used to study decision-making, including in addiction and other clinical conditions. **Computational models** split each person's choices into the processes behind them: how quickly they learn from wins and from losses, how strongly they stick with a deck, and how much they explore.

```{=html}
<figure class="igt-play">
  <div class="igt-head"><span class="m">ORL + α</span> playing the Iowa Gambling Task <span class="live">live</span></div>
  <div class="igt-grid" aria-hidden="true"></div>
  <div class="igt-tally" aria-live="off"></div>
  <figcaption class="fig-note">This is <strong>ORL + α</strong>, the model this research introduces, choosing 100 cards right now in your browser, one mark per card. Decks A <i class="s rect k0"></i> and B <i class="s circ k1"></i> pay $100 a card but lose more over time; C <i class="s tri k2"></i> and D <i class="s diam k3"></i> pay $50 and come out ahead. Its settings are drawn from the middle half of those fitted to the 162 participants, so every visit brings a new player.</figcaption>
</figure>
```

I implemented three standard models and fit them to **162 healthy adults**, then tested a series of extensions, writing my predictions down before each analysis. The one that held up best restores **outcome curvature** to the ORL model: the felt size of a win or a loss grows more slowly than its dollar amount. **ORL + α** predicted held-out choices best of eight models, and on a second sample of **70 people**, all five predictions written in advance were met.

{{< include _alpha_fig.qmd >}}

No single model described everyone well, though. Different people were predicted best by different models, which led to the next project.

## Mixing models: stacking

::: status
exploratory · first sample of 162 · confirmatory test in progress
:::

Picking one winning model throws away what the others get right. **Stacking** ([Yao et al., 2018](https://doi.org/10.1214/17-BA1091)) keeps all of them: each choice gets a probability from a weighted average of the eight models' predictions, with the weights chosen to predict held-out choices as well as possible. When one model is badly wrong about a choice, the others catch it.

One shared mix predicted held-out choices better than the best single model, ORL + α, for **124 of 162** people (*z* = 7.3). On average it gave the choice a person actually made about **4% more probability**.

{{< include _weights_fig.qmd >}}

People also differ in their mix. Giving each person their own weights, pulled 70% of the way toward the shared mix, predicted better still (*z* = 4.3). The differences are real, but 100 choices are too few to pin down anyone's mix exactly.

## Switching between strategies

::: status
exploratory · confirmatory test in progress
:::

A fixed mix assumes a person's blend stays the same all session. A **switching** model lets one strategy be "in charge" of a run of choices before another takes over. It beat the fixed mix (*z* = 5.3), and it lost that edge when each person's choices were shuffled, so the gain depends on the order of the choices. The best fit redrew the strategy in charge about once every **19 trials**.

Whether people really switch is the open question. I'm now testing it, with a preregistered plan, in **440 new participants** from the same data pool, and on data simulated with no switching at all, to see whether the method finds "switching" where there is none.

## Next

### Tiny recurrent neural networks

::: status
planned
:::

Every model here builds in a learning rule. **Tiny recurrent neural networks**, with only a few units and no rule built in, can learn people's choices directly, and they often predict those choices better than classic models do ([Ji-An, Benna & Mattar, 2025](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09142-4)). Trained and tested on the same held-out choices as the models, they will show how much predictable structure ORL + α and the stacked mix still miss, and the strategies the networks learn can point to what is missing.

### EEG: whose prediction errors does the brain track?

::: status
in preparation
:::

With about 100 choices per person, behavior alone can only say so much about which strategy someone is using. Each model also makes a **prediction error** on every trial, and the brain's response to feedback, the **reward positivity**, tracks prediction errors ([Sambrook & Goslin, 2015](https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000006)). Testing whose prediction errors it follows, one model's or a blend, would give neural evidence on strategy that choices alone cannot.

A first test can use open data: 59 people who did the task, 200 choices each, during EEG recording ([Chávez-Sánchez et al., 2026](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-026-06662-0)), with the analysis preregistered before the EEG is examined. A study of my own would follow, with a longer task or two sessions so that each person makes more choices.

## Data

All analyses use the open "many labs" Iowa Gambling Task data pool ([Steingroever et al., 2015](https://osf.io/8t7rm)).
